article_title: Hayabusa2 Flies About 10 Kilometers From Asteroid Torifune, and Its First Images Reveal a Two-Lobed Contact Binary
summary: Approved with one correction: the completed flyby, ~10 km distance, contact-binary finding, instruments, velocity, size, and 2031/1998 KY26 details all trace to cited sources; the '1998 KY26 enter orbit and attempt to land' detail attributed to EarthSky is not supported by that source.

findings.message: The 'Why It Matters' passage states that at the 2031 rendezvous with 1998 KY26 'the spacecraft is expected to enter orbit and attempt to land on the surface, according to EarthSky.' The cited EarthSky snapshot (source-2) does not say this; it states only that Hayabusa2 'should arrive at the asteroid in 2031.' The Debrief (source-3), cited in the same sentence for the 2031 rendezvous, likewise says only that the visit is 'expected to occur in 2031' and contains no orbit/landing language. This is a subordinate embellishment in the body, not the headline, summary, or lead, so it is filed as a correction rather than a rejection.
findings.details: EarthSky snapshot: 'the space probe is headed for the tiny asteroid 1998 KY26. The asteroid is just 36 feet (11 meters) in diameter. Hayabusa2 should arrive at the asteroid in 2031.' No 'enter orbit' or 'land' language present in either source.

content_preview.title: Hayabusa2 Flies About 10 Kilometers From Asteroid Torifune, and Its First Images Reveal a Two-Lobed Contact Binary
content_preview.summary: Japan's Hayabusa2 completed a successful July 5 flyby of asteroid Torifune, passing about 10 km away and returning first optical and thermal images that show a two-lobed contact binary.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

Japan's Hayabusa2 spacecraft has completed its high-speed pass of the near-Earth asteroid Torifune, and the first images beamed home show a double-lobed body that scientists describe as a contact binary. "On 5 July 2026 at 18:30 JST (error margin: ±1 second), Hayabusa2 successfully performed a flyby of Torifune," [JAXA said](https://global.jaxa.jp/press/2026/07/20260706-3_e.html) in a release dated July 6. editor_notes.content_quality: Well-structured News piece (600 words, within the 400-1200 News range). Clear sections (Overview, What We Know, What the Images Show, Why It Matters, What We Don't Know) and appropriate technical depth for a mission-update story. Correctly frames this as the delivery of results promised by the June 24 setup piece, with a link back to that prior coverage.
editor_notes.source_verification: All 5 source snapshots were decompressed from sources/2026-07/<slug>/ and read from disk (no re-fetch). source-0.html.gz (JAXA press release, July 6, global.jaxa.jp) CONFIRMED: the flyby quote 'On 5 July 2026 at 18:30 JST (error margin: +/-1 second), Hayabusa2 successfully performed a flyby of Torifune' verbatim; the '18:35 JST ... confirmed from ground communications to be operating normally' claim; the ~10 km TIR imaging distance; release of both the ONC-T optical and TIR thermal images; and the 'only part of the data ... has been transmitted to Earth. The remaining data will be transmitted to the ground during future operations' quote verbatim. source-1.html.gz (Space.com) CONFIRMED: 1,475-foot (450-meter) size, 62 million miles (100 million km) from Earth, the 'much cooler in what appear to be shadowed regions ... much warmer where the surface faces the sun' TIR quote verbatim, and the 'two-headed' characterization. source-2.html.gz (EarthSky) CONFIRMED: 6 miles (10 km) distance; the 'two rubble piles joined together, or what astronomers call a contact binary' quote verbatim; the 'gray body with two roundish lobes and a narrow waist covered in small bumps' description (drawn from EarthSky's image alt text 'Gray rock object with 2 roundish gray lobes and a narrow waist, totally covered with small bumps'); and 'JAXA is still acquiring this data, so expect more revelations.' EarthSky did NOT support the 'enter orbit and attempt to land on the surface' detail attributed to it (see findings) — it says only that Hayabusa2 'should arrive at the asteroid in 2031.' source-3.html.gz (The Debrief) CONFIRMED: 'traveling at speeds approaching 5 kilometers per second' verbatim, the 1998 KY26 visit 'expected to occur in 2031,' and the planetary-defense/deflection framing; it contains no orbit/landing language for KY26. source-4.html.gz (JAXA press release, June 9) CONFIRMED: the 'acquire fundamental data for the technology required to accurately guide a probe to impact with small celestial bodies' quote verbatim and the ~5 km/s planned flyby velocity.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: Central thesis is fully sourced: the completed July 5 flyby, ~10 km closest imaging distance, ~5 km/s velocity, 450 m size, two-lobed contact-binary finding, ONC-T/TIR instruments, thermal contrast, and 2031/1998 KY26 rendezvous all trace to cited sources. Critically, the 'contact binary' characterization is attributed to EarthSky and Space.com, not overstated as a JAXA conclusion — JAXA's own release does not use that term. The article correctly distinguishes the planned ~1 km flyby (June 9 release) from the ~10 km actual imaging distance (July 6 release) without conflating them. One subordinate claim ('enter orbit and attempt to land on the surface' at the 2031 KY26 rendezvous) is misattributed to EarthSky, which does not support it; filed as a correction.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and professional throughout. No sensationalism, no AI self-reference. Attributions are precise and per-claim.
editor_notes.originality: Genuinely new substance versus the June 24 setup piece (2026-06/24-japans-hayabusa2-sets-july-5-...). The prior article only announced the upcoming flyby and mission background; this reports the completed pass, the spacecraft's healthy post-flyby status, the first ONC-T optical and TIR thermal images, and the confirmed two-lobed contact-binary shape. This is a substantive update to a developing story, not a rehash.
concerns: One misattributed subordinate claim: 'the spacecraft is expected to enter orbit and attempt to land on the surface' at 1998 KY26 is attributed to EarthSky, which does not support it (nor does The Debrief). Filed as a correction. The underlying 2031 rendezvous itself is well-sourced.
recommendations: For future mission-update pieces, keep forward-looking operational details (orbit insertion, landing/touchdown plans) tied to a source that explicitly states them, rather than appending them to a source that only confirms the arrival date.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: High-quality, well-sourced update that delivers the genuinely new results of the Torifune flyby. All headline, summary, and lead claims are sourced and correctly attributed to JAXA and secondary outlets without overstatement. A single misattributed subordinate detail warrants APPROVE_WITH_CORRECTIONS so readers see a public corrections trail; it does not touch the central thesis and is not severe enough to reject.
